item.title: Fixing Bash Script Directory Changes: Keep Your Terminal Location
item.description:
“Fixing Bash Script Directory Changes: Keep Your Terminal Location”

Why Scripts Don’t Change Your Terminal’s Directory

When you run a script using ./your_script.sh or bash your_script.sh, a new subshell process is created. Inside this subshell, the cd command successfully changes the directory. However, once the script completes, the subshell terminates, and you are returned to your original shell, which remains in its initial directory. The changes made in the subshell are lost.

When constructing collections within PowerShell scripts, the use of the increment assignment operator (+=) to add elements can lead to significant performance degradation, especially as collection sizes grow. This iterative recreation process becomes a bottleneck.

item.title: PowerShell: Performance Impact of Array Increment Assignment
item.description:
“PowerShell: Performance Impact of Array Increment Assignment”

When constructing collections in PowerShell, particularly within loops, using the increment assignment operator (+=) can lead to significant performance degradation. This is due to how PowerShell handles arrays – they are immutable, meaning their size cannot change after creation. Every time += is used, PowerShell recreates the entire collection, appending the new item. This process becomes increasingly resource-intensive as the collection grows.

Why is += Inefficient?

The core of the inefficiency lies in this operation: $Collection = $Collection + $NewObject. For each iteration of a loop, PowerShell must allocate memory for a new array, copy all existing elements from the old array, and then add the new object. This repeated creation and copying is a major bottleneck.

item.title: Shebang Line in Python Scripts: Purpose and Usage
item.description:
“Shebang Line in Python Scripts: Purpose and Usage”

The initial line of a script, starting with #!, commonly referred to as the “shebang,” “hashbang,” or “pound bang,” serves a critical purpose in Unix-like operating systems. It’s an interpreter directive that informs the system’s program loader which interpreter should be used to execute the script. For Python, this line is typically #!/usr/bin/env python or #!/usr/bin/env python3.

This directive is essential when you intend to run a Python script directly from the command line, like ./my_script.py, rather than explicitly invoking the interpreter, such as python my_script.py.
